courseDescription: A comprehensive journey through the art and science of public speaking. This course provides a structured workflow for planning, building, and delivering impactful speeches. From managing stage fright and analyzing your audience to mastering vocal variety and handling professional Q&A, you will develop the confidence and technical skills required to communicate effectively in any setting.
targetLearner: Individuals seeking to build foundational speaking skills through a concept-first approach, focusing on professional and public lecture styles.

projects.project_description: Throughout this project, you will design, draft, and deliver a comprehensive 5-7 minute persuasive speech or business pitch. You will move from initial audience analysis and topic selection through research, structuring, and slide design, culminating in a recorded performance and a strategy for handling follow-up questions.
projects.final_deliverable: A complete Speaking Portfolio containing a detailed speech outline, professional slide deck, a high-quality video recording of the delivery, and a 'Q&A Preparedness' document.

units.title: Foundations of Speaking
units.description: Establish the psychological, ethical, and relational groundwork of public speaking. This unit focuses on the speaker-audience dynamic, strategies for managing anxiety, and the essential role of active listening and feedback.

lectures.title: The Speaking Situation
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the fundamental components of any speech event, establishing the relationship between the speaker, the message, and the audience within a specific context.

sessions.title: Speaker, Message, and Audience
sessions.description: This session introduces the rhetorical triangle, illustrating how the speaker's intent, the clarity of the message, and the audience's characteristics interact. You will learn to identify these three core elements in any communication scenario, enabling you to build a foundation for strategic speech planning that prioritizes the listener's perspective.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the traditional view of public speaking as a 'one-way performance.' Instead, frame it as a dynamic transaction between three distinct points: the Speaker, the Message, and the Audience. This is the 'Rhetorical Triangle.' On the whiteboard, draw an equilateral triangle and label the vertices. Explain that if any one side is neglected—for instance, if a speaker is brilliant but ignores the audience's specific needs—the entire structure of communication collapses. This conceptual shift is vital because it moves the learner's focus away from internal performance anxiety and toward the external mechanics of connection.

Begin with the 'Speaker' vertex. Don't just define the speaker as the person talking; define them as the 'Ethos' or the source of intent. Use the whiteboard to list 'Intent' and 'Persona.' Explain that the speaker brings a specific history and motivation to the stage. A common misconception here is that the speaker should be a 'blank slate' or a 'perfect professional.' Clarify that the most effective speakers are those who understand their own relationship to the topic—why they care and why they are the right person to deliver this specific message right now.

Move to the 'Audience' vertex. This is the most critical point for a concept-first lecture because learners often treat the audience as a monolithic block. On the board, write 'Expectations' and 'Knowledge Level.' Use the example of a scientist explaining a breakthrough: if the audience is a group of peers, the message requires data; if it's a group of investors, it requires a value proposition. The key insight here is that the audience effectively 'co-authors' the speech. If the speaker doesn't calibrate the message to the audience's baseline, no communication occurs. This prevents the error of 'information dumping' by forcing the speaker to define their listener first.

Connect the two to the 'Message' vertex. The message is not just the script; it is the bridge. Write 'Clarity' and 'Structure' under this vertex. Explain that the message must be the logical result of the Speaker’s intent meeting the Audience’s needs. If the speaker wants to persuade (intent) a skeptical group (audience), the message must prioritize evidence over emotion. This demonstrates the interdependency of the triangle. To solidify this, introduce a short practice moment: write a brief excerpt from a generic speech on the board and ask learners to pinpoint exactly where the 'bridge' breaks—is the speaker too self-focused, or is the message too complex for the room?

Conclude by having the learners draft a single sentence for a hypothetical scenario, such as a classroom presentation. The goal is to force them to synthesize the three elements into one 'Strategic Intent' statement: 'I (Speaker) want to explain X (Message) to my classmates (Audience) so that they can do Y.' This exercise reveals whether the learner understands that public speaking is an act of utility rather than just an act of talking. It sets the foundation for the entire course by establishing that every technical skill learned later—voice, slides, or eye contact—is merely a tool to keep this triangle balanced.

tasks: Identify the speaker, message, and audience in a short written excerpt from a speech.
Draft a one-sentence description of how these three elements interact for a hypothetical classroom presentation.

sessions.title: Context and Occasion
sessions.description: This session explores the physical, social, and psychological environment in which a speech occurs. You will learn to adapt your approach based on the formality and constraints of the setting, ensuring your message is appropriate and effective for the specific 'where' and 'when' of your talk.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transforming the abstract concept of 'speaking' into a localized event. The core philosophy of this session is that a speech never exists in a vacuum; it is physically and psychologically tethered to its environment. Start by drawing a large rectangle on the whiteboard representing the 'Context' that surrounds the rhetorical triangle from the previous session. Explain that context is the invisible filter through which an audience receives a message. If the speaker ignores the context, the message will feel 'deaf' to the room, regardless of how well-written it is. The primary goal here is to shift the learner's focus from internal performance anxiety to external environmental awareness.

Transition to the physical layer of context by sketching two contrasting icons: a megaphone in an open park and a desk lamp in a small conference room. Use this to illustrate the 'Physics of Presence.' In a park, the speaker must contend with competing stimuli—wind, passing cars, the lack of walls to contain sound. This requires more expansive gestures and vocal projection. Conversely, in a conference room, these same behaviors would feel aggressive and overwhelming. The logic here is that the 'where' dictates the 'how much' of your delivery. Help the learner see that environmental factors like lighting, temperature, and seating arrangements are not just logistical details but rhetorical constraints that determine how much energy a speaker must exert to maintain the audience's attention.

Now, layer on the 'Occasion'—the social and psychological climate. This is where many speakers fail by bringing the wrong 'energy' to the room. Draw a scale on the board ranging from 'Ritualistic/Formal' to 'Spontaneous/Informal.' Use the example of a wedding toast versus a business pitch to show how the occasion acts as a contract between the speaker and the audience. At a wedding, the audience expects sentiment and shared history; in a pitch, they expect efficiency and data. A common mistake is using a 'one-size-fits-all' tone. To prevent this, explain that the occasion defines the 'Rules of Engagement.' The teacher should emphasize that respecting the occasion is the highest form of audience analysis because it proves the speaker understands why everyone has gathered.

Introduce a brief mental exercise where the learner must imagine delivering a speech about 'Innovation' in a sterile hospital hallway versus a high-tech startup lounge. Ask them to identify which specific words or volume levels would change. This practice is designed to reveal the learner's intuitive grasp of 'appropriateness.' It moves the lesson from theory to a tactical decision-making process. The goal is for the learner to realize that the 'perfect speech' doesn't exist; only the 'perfect speech for this specific moment' exists.

Conclude by discussing 'Psychological Context'—the mood of the audience before you even step on stage. If an audience just came from a long, exhausting meeting, your context is one of fatigue. If they are there to celebrate a win, your context is one of high energy. Teach the learner to 'read the room' as the final step in preparation. The takeaway should be a framework: before writing a single word, the speaker must ask: Where am I? Why are we here? And what is the collective mood? This creates a strategic foundation that ensures the speech feels 'live' and relevant rather than canned or disconnected.

tasks: List three environmental factors that could impact a speech in a large outdoor park versus a small conference room.
Explain how the 'occasion' (e.g., a wedding vs. a business pitch) changes the expected tone of a speaker.

sessions.title: Ethics in Speaking
sessions.description: This session examines the moral responsibilities of a public speaker, including honesty, plagiarism prevention, and respect for diversity. You will gain a framework for making ethical choices during research and delivery, which is critical for maintaining long-term influence and personal integrity.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by reframing ethics from a list of 'don'ts' to a foundational asset of public influence. The core concept to establish is that a speaker's power is a borrowed resource given by the audience; once the ethical bond is broken through dishonesty or manipulation, the speaker's ability to effect change vanishes. On the whiteboard, I will draw a 'Bridge of Trust' connecting the speaker to the audience. This bridge is built on the pillars of honesty and transparency. I’ll explain that public speaking is not just about performance, but about the social contract between the communicator and the listener. The most important takeaway here is that ethics are not a constraint on your creativity, but the very floor that allows your message to stand.

Moving into the specifics of 'Intellectual Integrity,' I will tackle the common misconception that plagiarism is only about copying word-for-word. I’ll use the whiteboard to categorize three levels of ethical risk: global plagiarism (the wholesale theft), patchwork plagiarism (the 'franken-speech' approach), and the most subtle—incremental plagiarism, where a speaker fails to give credit for a specific quote or idea. I want to emphasize that even if a speaker's intentions are good, failing to cite a source correctly erodes their perceived competence. We will walk through the logic that citing others actually makes a speaker look *more* authoritative and well-researched, rather than less original, effectively reframing the fear students often have about sharing the spotlight with other experts.

Next, we address the 'Ethics of Evidence.' I will introduce the concept of 'cherry-picking'—the act of selecting only the data that supports your point while ignoring contradictory evidence. This is a crucial moment to discuss the difference between 'persuasion' and 'manipulation.' Using a visual spectrum on the board, I'll show how valid persuasion relies on logical reasoning and holistic data, whereas manipulation relies on omission and deception. I'll warn against the temptation to use a shocking statistic out of context just to get a reaction, explaining that while it might win a moment of attention, it risks a lifetime of professional credibility if discovered. This leads into our first practice task: analyzing a short text for these subtle breaches, which forces the learner to develop a 'critical eye' not just for others, but for their own future research habits.

We conclude by discussing the 'Social Responsibility' of the speaker, focusing on respect for diversity and the avoidance of dehumanizing language. The logic here is pragmatism as much as morality: if you alienate a portion of your audience through stereotypes or insensitive framing, you have failed at the primary goal of communication—connection. I'll explain that 'Inclusive Language' isn't about being 'politically correct,' but about being accurate and professional. To solidify these concepts, the final exercise asks learners to draft their own 'Speaker's Code of Ethics.' This isn't just a writing task; it's a diagnostic to see if they can synthesize honesty, credibility, and respect into a personal mission statement. This personal code serves as a guardrail for all subsequent speeches in this course, ensuring that as they gain technical skills in delivery and persuasion, those skills remain grounded in a consistent ethical framework.

tasks: Analyze a short text to identify potential ethical breaches such as cherry-picking data or lack of citation.
Write a personal 'Speaker's Code of Ethics' consisting of three guiding principles.

sessions.title: Credibility
sessions.description: This session defines 'Ethos' and breaks down the components of competence, character, and goodwill. You will learn how to establish and maintain trust with an audience from the moment you begin, laying the groundwork for a persuasive and authoritative presence.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This session addresses the concept of 'Credibility' not as a fixed personality trait, but as a dynamic perception managed by the speaker. We begin by introducing the Aristotelian concept of 'Ethos.' Rather than just defining it as 'reputation,' the instructor should visualize a three-legged stool on the whiteboard, with each leg representing one of the core components: Competence (what you know), Character (who you are), and Goodwill (how much you care about the audience). The key teaching point here is that an audience is constantly scanning for these markers; if even one leg of the stool is missing, the speaker's authority collapses.

To unpack 'Competence,' the lecture should clarify that this doesn't require being the world's leading expert. Instead, it’s about 'situational mastery.' The instructor should explain how subtle cues—such as citing a reliable source early or mentioning personal experience with the topic—signal to the audience that the speaker is a safe guide for the journey. A common pitfall for beginners is over-explaining their resume, which can come off as insecurity; the goal is to weave competence into the narrative naturally so the audience feels informed rather than lectured at.

Next, the focus shifts to 'Character' and 'Goodwill,' which are often the most overlooked elements. Character is about perceived honesty and integrity—do you practice what you preach? Goodwill is even more tactical: it is the speaker’s ability to demonstrate that they have the audience's best interests at heart. The instructor should illustrate this using the 'Bridge' analogy—a speaker can be a genius, but if they haven't built a bridge of empathy to the listener, the message will never cross. We address the 'Skeptical Audience' scenario here, showing how a simple acknowledgment of the audience's concerns or a shared value can transform an adversarial atmosphere into a cooperative one.

For the practice phase, the instructor prompts the learners to analyze the 'Introduction' phase of a speech. The task isn't just to list credentials, but to identify the specific moment a speaker 'earned' the right to be heard. Why did you trust them by minute two? This leads into the role-play exercise where learners must draft an opening statement for a difficult scenario, such as delivering bad news to a team. The objective of this exercise is to reveal that credibility is won or lost in the first sixty seconds, and that leading with 'Goodwill' is often the most effective way to disarm a skeptical room.

We conclude by reinforcing that credibility is a 'borrowed' asset that must be maintained throughout the speech. The instructor should visualize a 'trust meter' on the board that fluctuates based on the speaker's transparency and accuracy. The session ends by connecting this back to the ethical framework discussed previously: credibility is the external perception of the speaker’s internal ethics. This transition prepares the learner to move from the theory of 'the speaker' to the practical application of building 'the message' in the next unit.

tasks: Identify three ways a speaker can demonstrate competence during their introduction.
Role-play an opening statement that builds immediate goodwill with a skeptical audience.

lectures.title: Speech Anxiety
lectures.description: This lecture addresses the psychological and physiological aspects of stage fright, providing evidence-based techniques to transform nervous energy into focused performance.

sessions.title: Why We Get Nervous
sessions.description: This session deconstructs the 'fight or flight' response and the common fears associated with public speaking, such as the fear of judgment. You will understand the biological roots of performance anxiety, helping you realize that being nervous is a normal, manageable physical state rather than a sign of failure.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by reframing the concept of 'nerves' from a psychological failure to a biological success. Start by drawing a simple diagram of the brain on the whiteboard, highlighting the amygdala. Explain that public speaking anxiety is actually a 'false alarm' triggered by an ancient survival mechanism—the fight-or-flight response. Use the metaphor of a smoke detector that goes off because of burnt toast rather than a house fire; the body is simply preparing for a high-stakes social encounter by flooding the system with adrenaline. This biological grounding is crucial because it removes the stigma of 'weakness' and moves the learner toward a technical understanding of their own physiology.

Transition to the social aspect of this response by discussing the 'fear of the tribe.' Explain why being the center of attention feels dangerous: for our ancestors, being stared at by a group often preceded social exclusion or physical threat. On the whiteboard, list common fears like 'judgment,' 'making a mistake,' or 'appearing foolish.' Connect these back to the biological roots, showing that our brains perceive a quiet audience as a potential predator. This helps the learner realize that their anxiety isn't a reaction to the speech itself, but to the vulnerability of being observed, which is a universal human experience.

Introduce the 'Illusion of Transparency' through a diagnostic exercise. Ask the learners to list their top three physical symptoms—perhaps racing hearts, sweaty palms, or shaky hands. On the whiteboard, create two columns: 'Internal' (the storm inside) and 'External' (what the audience actually sees). Most learners are surprised to find that while they feel like their heart is pounding through their chest, the audience usually only sees a slightly faster blink rate or a subtle hand movement. This visualization exercise is designed to break the feedback loop where the speaker worries about their anxiety being visible, which in turn makes them more anxious.

Address the common misconception that professional speakers don't get nervous. Explain the concept of 'Arousal Reappraisal'—the idea that the physical sensations of anxiety and excitement are nearly identical. Instead of trying to 'calm down' (which is difficult when your body is in high gear), the goal is to acknowledge the energy. Illustrate this on the board as a bridge: one side is 'Anxiety' (negative/high energy) and the other is 'Excitement' (positive/high energy). It is much easier to cross that bridge than to drop down into 'Calm' (low energy). 

Conclude by reinforcing that the goal of this unit isn't to eliminate the butterfly feelings, but to 'get them to fly in formation.' Use the whiteboard to summarize the session's logic: Biology triggers the response, Social Fear amplifies it, but Awareness and Categorization (Internal vs. External) provide the control. This prepares the learner for the next session on cognitive restructuring, having first demystified the physical 'beast' they are facing.

tasks: List your top three physical symptoms of anxiety when speaking.
Categorize these symptoms into 'internal' (only you know) and 'external' (the audience might see) to gain perspective.

sessions.title: What Actually Helps
sessions.description: This session moves past common myths like 'imagining the audience in their underwear' to focus on cognitive restructuring and visualization. You will acquire practical cognitive tools to reframe anxiety as excitement, which is the first step toward building genuine confidence in high-pressure situations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by directly challenging the folklore of public speaking. Draw a large 'X' over the cliché of 'imagining the audience in their underwear' on the whiteboard. Explain that this common advice is not only ineffective but distracting, as it forces the speaker to focus on a bizarre mental image rather than the message or the audience's needs. The core concept here is cognitive restructuring: we aren't trying to suppress feelings, but to change our relationship with them. Use the whiteboard to illustrate the 'Arousal Spectrum,' showing that physiological symptoms like a racing heart or sweaty palms are nearly identical for both 'Fear' and 'Excitement.' The primary difference lies in the cognitive label we attach to that physical state.

Introduce the 'Anxiety Reappraisal' technique. Instead of telling yourself to 'calm down'—which is a high-effort attempt to jump from a high-arousal state (anxiety) to a low-arousal state (calmness)—teach the learner to say 'I am excited.' On the whiteboard, draw a bridge connecting Anxiety to Excitement, noting that both are high-energy states. Explain that this mental pivot allows the speaker to harness their adrenaline rather than fighting it. This is the 'Reframing' logic: the body is simply preparing for a performance, providing the energy needed to be dynamic. Address the common misconception that professional speakers don't get nervous; clarify that they simply label their nerves as 'game-day readiness.'

Transition to the concept of Visualization as a proactive rehearsal tool. Contrast 'worry' (visualizing failure) with 'strategic visualization' (rehearsing success). Draw a timeline of a speech opening on the board. Explain that the first 30 seconds are the most critical for confidence. Guide the learner through the process of mental mapping: seeing the room, feeling the firm ground under their feet, hearing the first sentence come out clearly, and noticing a positive reaction from a specific listener. This isn't 'positive thinking' in a vacuum; it is a neurological 'dry run' that reduces the novelty of the situation and lowers the brain's threat response. Emphasize that the visualization must be specific and sensory-rich to be effective.

End by integrating these two tools into a pre-performance routine. Explain that the goal of this session's practice—relabeling and drafting a visualization script—is to move from a reactive victim of stage fright to an active manager of performance energy. Caution the learner against expecting nerves to disappear entirely. Instead, explain that the goal is to have 'butterflies flying in formation.' Use the whiteboard to summarize the shift: from 'What if I fail?' to 'How can I use this energy to serve the audience?' This shift in focus from self-protection to audience-service is the final, most powerful piece of the cognitive puzzle.

tasks: Practice a 'relabeling' exercise where you describe your physical arousal as 'energy' or 'excitement'.
Draft a 30-second visualization script for a successful speech opening.

sessions.title: Practice Routines
sessions.description: This session introduces structured preparation methods, including the 'incremental rehearsal' technique. You will learn how to practice effectively rather than just repeating mistakes, ensuring that your preparation leads to mastery and reduces the uncertainty that fuels anxiety.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the internal mental shifts of the previous sessions to the external, systematic rigor of preparation. The core philosophy here is that anxiety is often a symptom of uncertainty; by replacing 'repetition' with 'structured rehearsal,' we eliminate the variables that cause speakers to panic. I begin by drawing a clear distinction on the board between 'reading over notes' and 'active rehearsal.' Most learners fall into the trap of passive review, which creates a false sense of competence. To break this, we introduce the 'Incremental Rehearsal' model, visualizing it as a staircase where each step adds a layer of complexity—starting with just the ideas, then moving to specific phrasing, and finally to physical delivery.

We start the whiteboard mapping with 'Phase 1: The Conceptual Run-through.' This is where I explain that the speaker should never memorize words initially, as forgetting a single word can trigger a total cognitive freeze during the actual speech. Instead, the focus should be on the 'Logical Spine' of the speech. I illustrate this by drawing a simple flowchart of a 2-minute introduction: Hook -> Thesis -> Roadmap. The goal of this phase is for the learner to be able to talk through the points naturally, even if the wording changes slightly each time. This builds 'cognitive flexibility,' ensuring that if they get distracted on stage, they can find their way back to the logic rather than searching for a lost sentence.

Next, we address the 'Middle-Out' strategy for rehearsal. I warn learners about the 'Front-Loading' trap—practicing the introduction fifty times while the conclusion remains shaky. To solve this, we visualize a 3-day schedule. Day 1 is for 'Segment Isolation,' where we pick the most difficult paragraph (often the transition or a complex data point) and practice only that. This prevents the fatigue of starting from the beginning every time. On the whiteboard, I map out how a 2-minute speech should be broken into 30-second modules, treated as independent 'LEGO bricks' that can be perfected individually before being snapped together.

I then introduce a low-stakes practice moment to reveal common pitfalls. I ask the learners to pick one specific paragraph from their planned introduction and deliver it to themselves with a focus solely on 'extemporaneous flow.' The common error here is 'perfectionist halting'—stopping the moment a mistake is made. I must emphasize that in rehearsal, they should practice 'recovering' rather than 'restarting.' If they trip on a word, they must find a way to finish the thought. This builds the muscle memory of resilience, which is the ultimate antidote to stage fright.

Finally, we wrap up by defining the 'Final Polish' phase, which occurs on Day 3 of their schedule. This is where we introduce environmental variables. I suggest practicing in different rooms or while standing up versus sitting down. I explain that the brain associates memory with environment, so by varying the practice space, the learner 'decouples' their speech from a specific safety zone, making it robust enough for the actual stage. The session concludes by reinforcing that mastery is not the absence of nerves, but the presence of a routine so deeply ingrained that it functions on autopilot when the adrenaline kicks in.

tasks: Create a 3-day practice schedule for a 2-minute introduction.
Perform a 'low-stakes' practice session focusing only on one specific paragraph.

sessions.title: Building Confidence
sessions.description: This session focuses on the long-term development of a 'growth mindset' regarding communication skills. You will learn how to use small successes to build a snowball effect of confidence, empowering you to volunteer for speaking opportunities and see yourself as an effective communicator.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final session of our deep dive into anxiety, we transition from managing acute symptoms to the strategic accumulation of speaking confidence. I begin by defining confidence not as the absence of fear, but as the presence of a 'growth mindset.' I illustrate this on the whiteboard by drawing two parallel paths: a fixed path where speaking is a static 'talent' (leading to avoidance), and a growth path where every word spoken is a 'repetition' toward mastery. The core idea here is that confidence is an earned byproduct of action, not a prerequisite for it. By framing public speaking as a plastic skill rather than a fixed personality trait, we lower the stakes for individual performances and focus on the trajectory of improvement.

To make this concrete, I introduce the 'Snowball Effect' of confidence. I visualize this on the board as a small spiral that expands outward. I explain that the primary reason people remain nervous is that they wait for a 'high-stakes' event (like a major presentation) to test their skills, which is the worst possible environment for learning. Instead, I guide the learners toward identifying 'micro-opportunities'—low-stakes environments such as asking a question in a meeting, giving a toast at dinner, or even speaking up more clearly during a phone call. The logic is that success in these small moments creates a physiological proof-of-concept that the brain uses to dismantle the 'danger' signals associated with speaking. I caution against the 'perfectionist trap' here, reminding them that the goal of these micro-moments is the act of speaking itself, regardless of whether the output was flawless.

Next, I pivot to the psychological technique of 'Positive Anchoring.' I ask the learners to recall a moment in their past where they communicated effectively—perhaps a one-on-one conversation where they felt understood or a moment they explained a complex idea to a friend. I want them to realize they already possess the mechanics of good communication. We use the whiteboard to deconstruct that successful moment: What was the environment? How did their body feel? By documenting these attributes, we create a mental 'home base' they can return to when feeling overwhelmed by a larger stage. This prevents the common misconception that professional speaking requires a different 'version' of oneself; it’s about scaling the authentic version that already succeeds in private.

I conclude by setting up the practice task, which serves as a diagnostic for their newfound mindset. I challenge them to look for one specific opportunity in the next 48 hours to be the first person to speak or to volunteer an opinion. The purpose of this exercise is to disrupt the habit of silence. I explain that the reflection they write afterward shouldn't just be about 'how well they did,' but about the realization that they survived the discomfort and emerged with more data for their growth. We end on the note that every confident speaker they admire is simply someone who has accumulated more of these micro-wins than they have, making mastery an inevitable result of persistence rather than a miracle of birth.

tasks: Identify one 'micro-opportunity' for speaking in your daily life this week.
Write a reflection on a past successful communication moment to reinforce a positive self-image.

lectures.title: Listening
lectures.description: This lecture emphasizes that public speaking is a two-way street, focusing on the skills required to be an effective audience member and a reflective speaker.

sessions.title: Active Listening
sessions.description: This session teaches the 'HURIER' model of listening (Hearing, Understanding, Remembering, Interpreting, Evaluating, Responding). You will develop the ability to process information more deeply, which will improve your own speaking by making you more aware of how audiences consume information.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that public speaking is a one-way performance. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple feedback loop, illustrating that a speech only exists if there is an ear to receive it. The goal is to shift the learner’s focus from 'what I say' to 'how they process.' Introduce the concept that the best speakers are actually the best listeners; by understanding the cognitive hurdles an audience faces, a speaker can tailor their delivery to bypass those barriers.

Introduce the HURIER model as a diagnostic framework for high-level listening. On the whiteboard, list the six stages: Hearing, Understanding, Remembering, Interpreting, Evaluating, and Responding. Explain 'Hearing' as the physiological prerequisite, but quickly pivot to 'Understanding' and 'Remembering' to explain that most information is lost within the first three minutes if the speaker lacks clarity. Emphasize that 'Interpreting' is where most communication breakdowns occur, as it involves decoding non-verbal cues and context. This logical progression shows the learner that listening is an active, multi-stage labor rather than a passive state, setting the foundation for why speech organization (Unit 2) will be so vital later.

Address the 'Listening Filters' that often distort a message before it is even fully processed. These include internal biases, emotional states, or even environmental noise. On the board, visualize these as a 'lens' between the speaker and the listener. Explain that a listener might 'Evaluate' a message too early—judging the speaker’s appearance or tone—which effectively shuts down the 'Understanding' phase. By identifying these filters, the learner realizes that as a speaker, they must work intentionally to 'clean the lens' for their audience through credibility and engagement.

Transition to a practical application moment by playing or describing a short three-minute speech. Instruct the learner not just to take notes, but to apply the HURIER model in real-time. The primary objective here is for the learner to distinguish between the 'content' (the facts) and the 'tone' (the emotional subtext). This exercise reveals whether the learner is stuck in the 'Hearing/Understanding' phase or if they can reach the 'Interpreting' phase, where the speaker's true intent resides. This depth of analysis is what separates a basic attendee from a master communicator.

Conclude by tying these listening skills back to the learner's development as a speaker. Explain that once you understand how hard it is to listen, you become a more empathetic and effective speaker. Use the whiteboard to summarize that 'Evaluating' and 'Responding'—the final stages of HURIER—are the benchmarks of a successful speech. If the audience cannot reach these stages because the 'Remembering' phase was too difficult, the speech has failed its purpose. This prepares the learner for the next session on Audience Attention, moving from the internal mechanics of listening to the external observation of engagement.

tasks: Listen to a 3-minute speech and summarize the main points and the underlying emotional tone.
Identify two common 'listening filters' that might bias your interpretation of a message.

sessions.title: Audience Attention
sessions.description: This session analyzes why audiences stop listening and how 'attention spans' function during a presentation. You will learn to recognize the signs of audience disengagement, providing you with the intuition needed to adjust your delivery or content in real-time during a speech.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this whiteboard session, we transition from the mechanics of personal listening to the broader concept of 'Collective Attention'. The core premise is that an audience's focus is not a constant state but a fragile resource that depletes over time. I will begin by drawing a 'Confidence/Attention Curve' on the whiteboard—a downward sloping line that typically drops off significantly after the first 10 minutes. This visual serves to demystify why speakers lose their audience: it's rarely a personal failing of the speaker's character, but rather a biological and cognitive limitation of the human brain. By framing attention as a 'battery' that the speaker must recharge, we lower the anxiety for the learner and shift the focus to strategic management.

We will then dive into the 'Invisible Cues' of disengagement. Instead of just looking for closed eyes or phones, I will illustrate on the board the subtle shifts in physical orientation—the 'Pelvic Tilt' away from the speaker, the 'Micro-Fidgets', and the loss of mirroring behavior. The goal here is to develop the learner's intuition to see a room as a living organism. I'll explain that a cough is rarely just a cough in a lecture; it's often a sign of a 'mental break' being taken by the group. We must address the misconception that a silent room is necessarily an attentive one. Sometimes, silence is actually cognitive 'opt-out', and the teacher needs to know how to distinguish between 'rapt silence' and 'bored stillness'.

To bridge the gap between observation and action, I will introduce the concept of the 'Attention Reset'. On the board, I'll map out three specific intervention types: the Vocal Shift (changing volume or pace), the Physical Shift (moving to a different part of the stage), and the Cognitive Shift (breaking the narrative flow with a question or a provocative visual). We will discuss why these work: they trigger the brain’s 'orienting reflex,' forcing the audience's subconscious to re-evaluate the environment and re-engage with the source of the stimulus. This isn't about being an entertainer; it's about being a conscious regulator of the room's energy.

We wrap up by practicing the 'Real-Time Pivot'. I will describe a hypothetical scenario where a speaker sees two people in the front row start whispering. Instead of ignoring it—which is the most common mistake—we will walk through how to use a 'purposeful pause' or a direct (but gentle) eye-contact shift to reclaim the space. The exercise of listing reset techniques is designed to give the speaker a 'toolkit of last resort' so that when they inevitably see the audience's attention wane, they don't panic, but instead deploy a calculated tactical adjustment to bring the focus back.

tasks: Observe a speaker and note at which points the audience's body language changes.
List three 'attention-reset' techniques a speaker can use when they notice a lapse in focus.

sessions.title: Giving Feedback
sessions.description: This session covers the principles of constructive criticism, focusing on the 'Sandwich Method' and descriptive rather than evaluative language. You will learn to provide specific, actionable feedback to peers, which fosters a supportive learning environment and sharpens your own critical eye for speech quality.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by reframing the act of giving feedback not as a social courtesy, but as a critical technical skill for the evaluator. The core concept to introduce here is that by identifying the mechanics of another person's speech, you are actually sharpening your own internal 'quality control' sensors. This shift in perspective helps move learners past the discomfort of critiquing a peer. I will start by using the whiteboard to contrast 'Evaluative' vs. 'Descriptive' language. Instead of a student saying 'Your speech was good'—which is a subjective judgment that offers no roadmap for improvement—I will demonstrate how to strip away the value judgment and describe the observable behavior: 'You maintained eye contact during the transition to your third point.' This makes the feedback objective and less threatening, ensuring the speaker focuses on the technique rather than their personal worth.

Next, I will introduce the 'Sandwich Method' on the board as a structural blueprint for constructive criticism: Positive reinforcement, constructive area for growth, and a forward-looking positive projection. However, the nuance I must emphasize here is the danger of the 'vague middle.' Many beginners provide a generic positive opening and a generic closing, burying a shallow critique in between. I will teach the instructor to model how to make the middle of the sandwich high-resolution. For example, rather than saying 'speak louder,' the feedback should be 'at the climax of your story, the volume dropped, making it difficult for the back row to catch the punchline.' This level of specificity transforms a complaint into a diagnostic tool.

To move into the application phase, I will facilitate a practice moment where I present a common, vague praise statement like 'You had great energy.' I will then challenge the class to 'reverse-engineer' it. What specific physical behaviors (pacing, hand gestures, vocal pitch) created that impression? This exercise is designed to reveal that 'energy' is not a magical aura but a sum of technical parts. By forcing students to translate feelings into descriptive observations, we prevent the common pitfall of feedback becoming a popularity contest. I'll illustrate this on the board by drawing a 'Feedback Funnel' that narrows down from broad impressions to specific, actionable data points.

Finally, we will address the pedagogical goal of fostering a supportive environment. I will explain that 'Constructive Criticism' is a misnomer if it doesn't provide a solution. Every identified weakness must be paired with an 'Actionable Pivot.' On the whiteboard, I will map out the 'Observation -> Impact -> Alternative' flow. If the observation is 'You looked at your notes for 80% of the speech,' the impact is 'The audience lost a sense of connection,' and the alternative is 'Try using bullet-pointed keywords instead of full paragraphs.' This ensures that the speaker leaves the session with a clear task list rather than a sense of defeat. This session concludes by emphasizing that the best critics often become the best speakers because they have trained their brains to see the invisible scaffolding of a presentation.

tasks: Write three constructive feedback comments for a sample speech using descriptive language.
Practice turning a vague 'That was good' into a specific, helpful observation.

sessions.title: Receiving Feedback
sessions.description: This session focuses on the emotional and cognitive resilience required to accept criticism. You will learn how to filter feedback to find actionable insights, ensuring that every speech you give—even the ones that feel like failures—contributes to your long-term improvement as a speaker.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by reframing the speaker's emotional relationship with feedback. Instead of viewing criticism as a personal verdict on talent, introduce the concept of 'Feedback as Raw Data.' Explain that in a public lecture context, a speaker’s growth isn't linear; it’s a series of iterations. The primary goal here is to help the learner build a 'psychological firewall'—separating their self-worth from the technical execution of a speech. Use the whiteboard to draw a filter icon, illustrating that not all feedback is created equal. Some is 'signal' (actionable, specific, and relevant), while some is 'noise' (subjective preferences or vague emotional reactions). The teacher should emphasize that the ability to receive feedback is a meta-skill that accelerates the acquisition of every other skill in this course.

Transition into the 'Emotional First Aid' for speakers. When receiving a critique, the natural biological response is defensiveness—the 'fight or flight' mechanism. Teach the learner to recognize the 'Sting'—that initial 10-second window of discomfort—and to simply breathe through it before responding. Address the common misconception that 'listening to feedback means agreeing with it.' On the whiteboard, map out the 'Accept-Discard-File' framework. A speaker accepts what is actionable, discards what is purely subjective or ill-informed, and files away what might be relevant for a different context or future goal. This logical sorting prevents the feeling of being overwhelmed and allows the learner to remain the 'CEO' of their own speaking style.

Introduce the concept of 'Active Clarification' as a tool for empowerment. Many learners feel like passive recipients of a judge's score. Instead, teach them to lead the debrief. If a critic says, 'Your middle section was confusing,' the teacher should demonstrate how to drill down with questions like, 'Was it the logic of the argument or the pace of my delivery that made it hard to follow?' By teaching the learner to ask for specific evidence, we transform a vague negative into a concrete technical problem that can be solved. Use the practice task of reviewing past feedback to help the learner identify one 'ghost'—a piece of criticism they've been carrying—and re-process it through this filter to find a single, manageable adjustment for their next appearance.

Conclude by discussing the 'Growth Loop.' Explain that the most effective speakers actually seek out the most critical audiences because they offer the fastest path to mastery. The logic here is that a 'failed' speech with a thorough debrief is infinitely more valuable than a 'safe' speech with no feedback. Encourage the learner to develop a 'thick skin but a thin filter'—being emotionally resilient to the delivery of the critique while being intellectually sensitive to the insights within it. The final practice of drafting clarifying questions is designed to shift the power dynamic back to the speaker, ensuring they leave every feedback session feeling like a researcher who has just collected a valuable new data point.

tasks: Review a piece of past critical feedback and identify one specific thing you can change in your next speech based on it.
Draft two clarifying questions you would ask a critic to better understand their perspective.

projects.stage_title: Topic Selection and Anxiety Management Plan
projects.stage_description: Identify a high-stakes speaking scenario (e.g., a board meeting or a public lecture) and define your core message. Create a personalized practice routine to address specific nervous triggers.
projects.deliverable_increment: A one-page project charter including the chosen speech topic, target audience profile, and a 3-step anxiety management strategy.

exams.title: Foundations of Speaking Comprehensive Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's understanding of the speaker-audience relationship, ethical principles, anxiety management strategies, and the mechanics of active listening and feedback.
sections: This exam covers the core theoretical and psychological components of Unit 1, testing the ability to identify ethical dilemmas, apply anxiety-reduction techniques, and analyze listening scenarios.
successCriteria: Correctly identify the components of the rhetorical triangle in varied scenarios.
Demonstrate knowledge of evidence-based anxiety management techniques.
Apply ethical standards to research and delivery vignettes.
Analyze audience listening patterns and propose engagement strategies.
Formulate constructive and specific feedback based on speech samples.

units.title: Planning the Speech
units.description: Shift into the logical planning phase. Learn how to conduct thorough audience analysis, gather high-quality supporting materials, and organize your ideas into a clear, logical framework.

lectures.title: Audience and Purpose
lectures.description: This lecture establishes the foundational strategy of any speech: defining exactly who you are speaking to and what you want to achieve with them.

sessions.title: Audience Analysis
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to research and segment your audience based on demographics, psychographics, and existing knowledge. You will learn to build an 'Audience Persona' that informs every subsequent choice in your speech. Mastering this ensures your message is relevant and resonant rather than generic, moving you toward your goal of professional influence.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin by grounding the concept of public speaking not as an act of self-expression, but as an act of service to the listener. In this concept-first approach, the primary logical anchor is that the audience is the destination, and your speech is the vehicle. To drive effectively, you must map the terrain. Introduce the 'Audience Persona' as a strategic tool rather than a mere list of facts. Explain that every word choice, joke, and data point in a speech is a variable, and 'Audience Analysis' is the process of solving for those variables. The core idea here is relevance: a speech that tries to speak to everyone ends up speaking to no one. 

Transition to the technical segmentation of an audience, starting with Demographics. Use the whiteboard to visualize these as the 'hard boundaries'—age, gender, education level, and professional role. Explain that these factors establish the baseline for language complexity and cultural references. However, caution against the trap of stereotyping; demographics tell you who is in the room, but they don't tell you what those people value. This realization should lead naturally into the deeper layer of Psychographics. 

Define Psychographics as the 'soft interior' of the audience: their values, beliefs, attitudes, and motivations. On the whiteboard, contrast a demographic fact (e.g., 'Senior Managers') with a psychographic insight (e.g., 'High fear of being disrupted by new technology'). Explain that while demographics help you avoid offending or confusing the audience, psychographics are what allow you to move and persuade them. The logic is simple: you cannot influence a person if you do not understand the internal incentives that drive their decision-making. 

Introduce the third pillar: Existing Knowledge and Expectations. This is where many novice speakers fail by either 'talking down' to experts or 'talking over' beginners. Use the whiteboard to draw a spectrum of expertise. Explain that identifying where the audience sits on this spectrum dictates how much jargon is permissible and how much foundational 'why' is needed. Address the misconception that more detail equals more authority; in reality, providing too much detail to a high-level executive suggests a lack of strategic prioritization, while providing too little to a technical team suggests a lack of competence. 

Wrap up by moving into the practical application. Guide the students through the process of synthesizing these three pillars into a singular 'Audience Persona.' For the first practice task involving corporate executives, prompt them to look beyond the job titles to find the hidden pressures of that role. For the second task regarding middle-schoolers and sustainable energy, the exercise is designed to reveal how to translate complex global issues into immediate, tangible experiences relevant to a 13-year-old’s life. The goal is for the learner to see that a 'great speech' is actually just a 'perfectly calibrated speech' for its specific target.

tasks: Draft a list of five demographic and three psychographic questions for a hypothetical audience of corporate executives.
Create an audience profile for a speech about sustainable energy aimed at middle-school students.

sessions.title: Adapting to the Audience
sessions.description: This session covers the practical strategies for adjusting your language, examples, and tone to match your audience profile. You will gain the ability to pivot your content to meet the specific needs and potential resistances of different groups. This is crucial for building the 'Audience-Centric' mindset required for effective public leadership.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by establishing the concept that a speech is not a fixed script, but a fluid bridge between the speaker's intent and the audience's reality. Explain that while the previous session focused on 'Who they are,' this session is about 'How we meet them there.' The core logic here is that your message exists in the listener's head, not your own; therefore, any technical jargon or misaligned tone acts as static on the line. Visualize this on the whiteboard by drawing a 'Content Filter'—on one side is your raw expertise, and on the other are the specific constraints of the audience persona (their vocabulary, their values, and their attention span).

Introduce the 'Translation Layer' technique. Use the example of a technical concept like 'blockchain' or 'quantum computing' to demonstrate how to strip a concept to its functional essence before rebuilding it with metaphors that resonate with specific groups. For a younger, tech-savvy audience, you might use gaming or peer-to-peer networking metaphors; for an older, less technical audience, you might use the analogy of a physical ledger or a community library card. The goal here is to show that simplification is not 'dumbing down,' but rather 'clearing the path' for understanding. Warn against the common mistake of over-simplifying to the point of condescension, which destroys rapport.

Transition into the 'Tone and Resonance' phase. Explain that the same set of facts can feel cold and clinical or warm and inspiring depending on the delivery and framing. Use the whiteboard to map out a 'Tone Spectrum' ranging from formal/authoritative to casual/collaborative. Explain that a speaker’s authority is granted by the audience, and it is gained by matching the level of formality expected in that specific context. For instance, a boardroom requires high-stakes precision, whereas a community center requires accessible empathy. The pivotal idea is that if the audience feels you don't speak their 'social language,' they will stop listening to your 'factual language.'

Address the challenge of a skeptical or hostile audience by introducing the 'Common Ground' principle. Instead of starting with a point of contention, teach the strategy of leading with a shared value or a mutually recognized problem. On the whiteboard, draw two overlapping circles: 'Speaker's Goal' and 'Audience's Current Belief.' The intersection is where you must start the speech. This prevents the 'defensive reflex' where listeners stop processing information the moment they feel challenged. Explain that rapport isn't about being liked; it's about being perceived as someone who understands the audience's perspective.

Conclude by guiding the learner through a mental rehearsal of pivoting content. Present a scenario where a presentation for software engineers suddenly needs to be given to the CFO. The underlying logic is to identify what the listener 'cares' about—the engineers care about the 'How' (stability/syntax), while the CFO cares about the 'Result' (ROI/risk). This illustrates that audience adaptation is ultimately a shift from features to benefits. Use a practice moment to have the learner identify three ways to shift their language from technical metrics to human-centric outcomes, highlighting that the core truth of the data remains the same, but the lens through which it is viewed changes entirely.

tasks: Rewrite a technical explanation of 'blockchain' for two different audiences: software engineers and retirees.
Identify three ways to build rapport with an audience that is known to be skeptical of your topic.

sessions.title: General Purpose
sessions.description: This session defines the four primary goals of public speaking: to inform, persuade, entertain, or commemorate. You will understand how identifying your primary driver prevents 'mixed messaging' and keeps your content focused. This clarity is the first step in moving from a novice speaker to a purposeful communicator.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin by framing the 'General Purpose' not as a creative choice, but as a strategic compass. I'll draw a large four-quadrant matrix on the board to visualize the primary drivers of public speaking: To Inform, To Persuade, To Entertain, and To Commemorate. The central concept here is that every decision a speaker makes—from word choice to slide design—must serve this primary driver. I’ll explain that most speaking failures stem from 'purpose drift,' where a speaker tries to be funny, educational, and demanding of action all at once, leading to a diluted message that leaves the audience confused about their takeaway.

First, we tackle the 'Informative' quadrant. The teacher should emphasize that the goal here is the transfer of knowledge with neutrality. I’ll use the analogy of a 'map-maker'—your job is to help the audience navigate a topic without telling them which destination to choose. A common pitfall for beginners is turning an informative speech into a subtle sales pitch. To prevent this, I'll illustrate how to maintain an objective tone and focus on clarity and comprehension over influence.

Next, we transition to 'Persuasion,' the most active quadrant. Here, the goal shifts from knowledge transfer to belief or behavior modification. I’ll visualize this as a 'bridgebuilder'—you are moving the audience from Point A (their current stance) to Point B (your desired stance). The teacher should contrast this sharply with the informative purpose: while information seeks to enlighten, persuasion seeks to advocate. We must address the misconception that persuasion is inherently manipulative; rather, it is about providing the logical and emotional scaffolding for the audience to make a decision.

Moving to 'Entertainment' and 'Commemoration,' I’ll group these as 'Experience-based' purposes. For 'To Entertain,' the priority is the audience's immediate emotional engagement and enjoyment—think of it as a 'performer' role. For 'To Commemorate,' the goal is to honor or mark a significant moment, acting as a 'vessel' for shared values. I will explain that even in professional settings, these purposes exist—such as an after-dinner speech or a retirement toast—and failing to recognize their unique requirements (like the need for storytelling and rhythm over data) can make a speaker seem cold or out of touch.

To solidify these concepts, we will engage in a diagnostic exercise. I'll present a neutral topic like 'Artificial Intelligence.' On the board, I'll demonstrate how the speech structure fundamentally mutates based on the purpose: an informative speech explains how neural networks function; a persuasive speech argues for stricter AI regulation; an entertaining speech tells humorous anecdotes about AI fails; and a commemorative speech honors the pioneers of the field. This exercise reveals that the 'topic' is just the raw material; the 'purpose' is the finished tool. We finish by challenging learners to categorize diverse speech titles, forcing them to detect the subtle linguistic cues that signal the speaker's true intent.

tasks: Categorize a list of five speech titles into their most likely general purpose category.
Write a short paragraph explaining how a single topic (e.g., 'Coffee') changes depending on whether the general purpose is to inform vs. to persuade.

sessions.title: Specific Purpose and Thesis
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to narrow a broad topic into a one-sentence specific purpose and a clear, debatable thesis statement. You will learn to draft a 'roadmap' sentence that guides the listener's expectations. Developing a sharp thesis is essential for maintaining audience attention and achieving structured clarity in your delivery.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by visualizing the transition from the 'General Purpose' discussed earlier to the 'Specific Purpose.' On the whiteboard, draw a large funnel. At the wide top, place the general purpose—for example, 'To Inform.' Explain that while this sets the mood, it lacks direction. The Specific Purpose is the neck of the funnel; it is a precise statement of what the speaker hopes to accomplish. It must be phrased from the audience's perspective: 'After my speech, the audience will be able to...' This shift in focus is the first conceptual hurdle for learners, as it moves the speech from being a self-centered performance to an audience-centered service.

Demonstrate how to construct a Specific Purpose statement using a three-part formula: the verb (to explain, to convince), the target audience (my team, the board of directors), and the precise goal (the benefits of the new software). Emphasize that a common mistake is being too broad or trying to accomplish multiple goals in one sitting. For instance, 'to inform the audience about the history of medicine and how to perform CPR' is a recipe for a cluttered, ineffective speech. Use the whiteboard to cross out 'and' statements, showing that a specific purpose must be singular and focused to ensure the speaker stays on track.

Transition to the 'Thesis Statement' as the logical evolution of the purpose. If the Specific Purpose is what you want to *do*, the Thesis is what you want to *say*. It is the 'DNA' of the speech. On the board, write a weak, factual thesis like 'Recycling is a process.' Contrast this with a strong, debatable, and actionable thesis: 'Implementing a mandatory office recycling program will reduce our waste costs by 20% and improve brand reputation.' This highlights the second major concept: a thesis must have 'teeth.' It should be a single, declarative sentence that encapsulates the main message and provides a 'roadmap' for the sub-points to follow.

Introduce a diagnostic exercise where learners are given a broad topic like 'Artificial Intelligence.' Ask them to first narrow it to a Specific Purpose (e.g., 'To persuade local business owners to adopt AI chatbots') and then into a Thesis (e.g., 'AI chatbots are an essential investment for local businesses because they provide 24/7 customer support while lowering operational overhead'). This exercise reveals if the learner is struggling with scope or clarity. Teachers should watch for 'roadmap' sentences that are too long or contain 'fluff' words that dilute the impact of the message.

Conclude by illustrating the 'Roadmap' function of the thesis. Show how a well-crafted thesis naturally predicts the body paragraphs of the speech. For example, if the thesis mentions 'cost savings' and 'reputation,' the audience now expects exactly two main sections. This internal logic provides the 'structured clarity' mentioned in the session goals, helping the speaker maintain control and the audience stay engaged. Warn against the 'Mystery Novel' approach where the thesis is hidden; in public speaking, clarity is kindness, and the thesis should be the beacon that guides the listener through the entire presentation.

tasks: Transform three broad topics into specific purpose statements and corresponding thesis statements.
Critique a set of 'weak' thesis statements and rewrite them to be more specific and actionable.

lectures.title: Research and Support
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on gathering the 'evidence' that gives your speech weight and authority, moving from abstract ideas to concrete proof.

sessions.title: Finding Credible Material
sessions.description: This session explores how to evaluate sources using the CRAAP test (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose). You will learn to distinguish between academic research, trade publications, and popular media. This builds the academic rigor necessary for high-stakes professional presentations and establishes your credibility as a speaker.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the act of research not as a chore, but as the construction of a speaker's 'Ethos' or character. The foundational concept to establish is that your audience grants you their time on the assumption that you are an expert on your topic for the duration of the speech. To maintain this trust, we must move beyond 'googling' and toward systematic evaluation. I will introduce the CRAAP test (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) as a mental filter. On the whiteboard, draw five large funnels. Each funnel represents one layer of the test. Explain that a piece of information must pass through all five to reach the 'podium.' This visual emphasizes that credibility is a compounding quality; it is not enough for a source to be 'accurate' if it is ten years out of date for a technology-focused speech.

Moving into the specific criteria, we focus on the distinction between 'Authority' and 'Accuracy.' Many speakers confuse the two. You might find an accurate fact on a random blog, but without authority, your audience has no reason to believe you didn't just make it up. Conversely, an authoritative figure can sometimes be wrong or biased. This is the moment to introduce the hierarchy of sources: academic peer-reviewed research at the top, followed by trade publications, and then popular media at the base. On the board, create a pyramid. Explain that while popular media is great for finding 'hooks' or stories, academic research provides the 'bedrock' evidence. A common pitfall for beginners is relying solely on the first page of search results. We counteract this by teaching the difference between primary sources (the original experiment or document) and secondary sources (the news article reporting on it). I want to emphasize that a high-stakes professional presentation requires moving as close to the primary source as possible to avoid the 'telephone game' effect of misinformation.

Now we pivot to the 'Currency' and 'Purpose' aspects. In a concept-first lecture, it is vital to explain that the 'shelf-life' of information varies. Historical data might be timeless (Currency is less critical), whereas economic or medical data might expire in months. For 'Purpose,' we tackle the nuance of bias. A source isn't necessarily 'bad' because it has a point of view, but a speaker must be aware of that intent to avoid being a mouthpiece for propaganda. We use the 'What is the goal of this author?' question as a diagnostic tool. If the purpose is to sell a product rather than inform, the evidence requires extra scrutiny.

To solidify these concepts, we move to a hands-on ranking exercise. I will present three hypothetical articles on a topic—perhaps something neutral like 'the effects of caffeine'—and ask the group to apply the CRAAP filters. The goal is to spark a debate on which one is the 'most credible.' This reveals the subjective nature of research: a source that is 'credible' for a casual speech at a social club might be 'unacceptable' for a board of directors meeting. We conclude by drafting a source list for a speech on 'The History of Space Exploration.' This allows learners to practice differentiating between a NASA technical report (Primary/Academic) and a National Geographic article (Secondary/Popular), ensuring they understand how to balance their research to build a speech that is both rigorously supported and engagingly told.

tasks: Evaluate three provided web articles using the CRAAP criteria and rank them by credibility.
List three primary and three secondary sources for a speech on 'The History of Space Exploration'.

sessions.title: Examples and Stories
sessions.description: This session teaches the 'Narrative Paradigm'—why stories are often more persuasive than facts alone. You will learn how to select and craft brief examples and extended narratives that illustrate your main points. This adds a human element to your speech, making your message memorable and emotionally resonant.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the 'Data-Logic Trap'—the common misconception among novice speakers that a speech is simply a delivery system for facts. To break this, we introduce Walter Fisher’s Narrative Paradigm. The core concept here isn't that stories are 'nice additions,' but that humans are inherently storytellers (homo narrans) who evaluate the world through narrative probability (does the story hang together?) and narrative fidelity (does it ring true to experience?). On the whiteboard, I draw a bridge where one pillar is 'Data' and the other is 'Action.' The bridge itself is 'Story.' Without the story, the audience understands the data but lacks the emotional bridge to move toward the desired action or belief.

Next, we differentiate between 'Brief Examples' and 'Extended Narratives.' I illustrate this by visualizing a magnifying glass: a brief example is a quick flash of reality—a specific name, a precise location—that grounds a general statement. An extended narrative, however, is a 'deep dive' that requires a character, a conflict, and a resolution. The most critical teaching point here is the 'Moment of Choice.' For a story to be persuasive, the protagonist must face a dilemma that mirrors the audience's own challenges. This prevents the story from being mere entertainment and transforms it into a functional tool for proof.

We then transition to the 'Hypothetical Example.' This is a vital tool when real-life data is confidential or when we are describing a future state. I guide the students through the 'What If' technique. The pitfall to avoid here is lack of detail; if a hypothetical example is too vague, it feels like a lie. I instruct the teacher to demonstrate how to use sensory details—sights, sounds, and specific feelings—to make a 'made-up' scenario feel concrete. The goal is to make the audience 'co-author' the example in their minds, which creates a higher level of buy-in than any dry statistic could achieve.

To move into the practice phase, we tackle 'The Resilience Map.' I ask students to outline a personal story not as a chronological list of events, but as a series of emotional beats: The Status Quo, The Disruption, The Struggle, and The New Normal. This exercise is designed to reveal if the student is over-sharing (the 'TMI' trap) or under-developing the conflict. We focus on the 'So What?'—the specific lesson or value that the story provides to the audience. This reinforces the concept-first lecture style by showing that the story exists to serve the concept, not the speaker's ego.

Finally, we address the integration of stories into the broader speech structure. A story should never exist in a vacuum; it needs 'connective tissue.' I demonstrate on the board how to 'Bookend' a speech—starting a story in the introduction and only revealing the resolution in the conclusion. This creates a 'Narrative Open Loop' that keeps the audience's attention high throughout the technical portions of the lecture. We conclude by emphasizing that while facts provide the skeleton of the speech, stories provide the flesh and the heartbeat, making the message humanly resonant.

tasks: Find a factual claim and draft a 30-second 'hypothetical example' to illustrate it.
Outline a personal story that could be used to support a point about 'resilience'.

sessions.title: Statistics
sessions.description: This session focuses on the ethical and effective use of numerical data. You will learn how to 'humanize' numbers so they aren't just dry data points, but meaningful insights for the audience. Mastery of this prevents 'death by data' and ensures your quantitative evidence actually supports your thesis.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this whiteboard-centric session, we move beyond the mere presence of data to the art of translating it. The core philosophy here is that statistics are not arguments in themselves; they are the raw materials that require 'humanization' to become persuasive tools. We begin by addressing the common pitfall of 'data dumping,' where a speaker overwhelms the audience with raw figures, leading to mental fatigue. To counter this, we introduce the concept of 'Social Scaling.' On the whiteboard, draw a single massive number, like '1.3 trillion dollars,' and then visually break it down into units that an individual can grasp—such as 'the cost of a cup of coffee for every person on Earth for a year.' This visualization teaches the learner that the value of a statistic lies entirely in its relatability.

Next, we transition into the ethical dimension of quantitative evidence. It is vital for a speaker to understand that numbers can be technically accurate yet profoundly misleading. We will use the whiteboard to illustrate how 'framing' affects perception. For example, explain the difference between saying a '10% mortality rate' versus a '90% survival rate.' While the mathematical fact is identical, the rhetorical impact is diametrically opposed. This helps prevent the learner from being manipulated by data or unintentionally manipulating their audience, establishing a foundation of integrity that is crucial for high-stakes professional speaking.

We then delve into the 'Contextual Anchor' technique. A number standing alone is a 'cold' fact. To 'warm' it up, we must place it next to a known entity. If a speaker says a new software update takes up 50 gigabytes, that may mean nothing to a non-technical audience. But if the speaker adds, 'That is roughly equivalent to 15,000 high-resolution photos,' the data gains weight. On the board, create a 'Context Map' where we link abstract metrics (liters, percentages, light years) to physical or temporal experiences (bathtubs, slices of a pizza, the length of a commute). This exercise ensures that the audience never has to do the math themselves, keeping their focus on the speaker’s message rather than mental arithmetic.

Finally, we engage in a diagnostic practice moment focused on 'Relatability Transformations.' The goal is for learners to take a dry, large-scale statistic and find its human equivalent. This reveals whether the learner truly understands the scale of their evidence or if they are just repeating what they read in a report. We conclude by emphasizing that in public speaking, 'less is more' regarding numbers. One well-humanized statistic is always more memorable than a slide full of spreadsheets. This session unlocks the ability to use quantitative data as a bridge to understanding rather than a barrier to engagement.

tasks: Take a large statistic (e.g., '1 trillion gallons of water') and create a comparison that makes it relatable to a person's daily life.
Identify two ways a statistic could be 'misleading' even if the number itself is technically accurate.

sessions.title: Testimony
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to incorporate expert and peer testimony to bolster your arguments. You will learn the mechanics of oral citations—how to give credit while maintaining the flow of your speech. Using testimony correctly builds your 'Ethos' and leverages the authority of others to support your goals.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final session of Unit 2, we transition from the cold hard facts of statistics and stories into the realm of 'Ethos'—the ethical appeal and credibility we gain by borrowing the authority of others. This is the concept of Testimony. To start the whiteboard session, I'll draw a bridge connecting the speaker to an 'Expert' and a 'Peer'. The core idea to land here is that your speech shouldn't just be 'you saying things'; it should be a synthesis of voices that validate your claims. I'll frame testimony not as a quote to be read, but as a strategic alignment that prevents the audience from questioning your personal biases.

We begin by differentiating between Expert Testimony and Peer Testimony, using the whiteboard to map out when each is most effective. Expert testimony is the 'heavy artillery'—it provides authority from researchers or specialists. However, I need to warn against the 'fallacy of irrelevant authority'—just because someone is a genius in physics doesn't make their testimony valuable in a speech about social psychology. Peer testimony, on the other hand, provides the 'human element' or 'street cred'. It’s the survivor of a disaster or the student who successfully used a study technique. The logical transition here is that experts provide the 'why' and peer testimony provides the 'relatability'. A common pitfall for new speakers is over-relying on experts, which can make a speech feel cold and elitist, or over-relying on peers, which makes it feel anecdotal and unscientific.

Next, we tackle the technical execution: the Oral Citation. On the whiteboard, I’ll demonstrate the 'Lead-in' technique. Most students make the mistake of dropping a quote like a heavy brick—silence, quote, silence—which disrupts the flow. I’ll show how to weave the source’s credentials directly into the sentence structure: 'As Dr. Aris Thorne, lead researcher at the Global Health Institute, noted in a 2023 report...' This builds the source's credibility before the audience even hears the information. We will practice 'credentialing'—the art of explaining why this person’s opinion matters in five words or less. This ensures the audience doesn't have to wonder why they should listen to the person being quoted.

To wrap up, we will conduct a brief exercise where students must take a single claim—for example, 'Consistent sleep schedules improve GPA'—and identify one expert source (like a neurologist) and one peer source (a high-achieving student). This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand the different functions of these voices: the neurologist explains the brain chemistry, while the student proves it’s achievable in a real-world context. I’ll conclude by emphasizing that testimony is about building a community of support around your argument, making it harder for the audience to dismiss your message as just one person's opinion.

tasks: Draft three different ways to introduce a quote from an expert in a speech.
Compare the effectiveness of an 'expert testimony' vs. a 'peer testimony' for a speech about the benefits of a specific study habit.

lectures.title: Organization
lectures.description: This lecture is the 'engineering' phase of speechwriting, where you assemble your research and purpose into a logical, easy-to-follow structure.

sessions.title: Main Points
sessions.description: This session explains how to select and word your main points to be discrete, balanced, and parallel. You will learn to limit yourself to 2-5 main points to ensure audience retention. This structural discipline is what separates a rambling talk from a professional presentation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by conceptualizing the 'Main Points' not just as items on a list, but as the structural pillars of a building. Explain that while a speaker might have dozens of insights, an audience's working memory is a finite resource. The core objective here is to introduce the 'Rule of Three to Five.' Using the whiteboard, draw a container representing the audience's mind and show how it overflows when ten disconnected ideas are poured in, versus how it neatly organizes three distinct clusters. Emphasize that the most common mistake for novice speakers is 'comprehensiveness over clarity'; clarify that leaving a good idea out is often a strategic win if it preserves the integrity of the primary message.

Transition to the criteria for selecting these points: they must be discrete and balanced. On the whiteboard, illustrate 'discrete' by drawing two non-overlapping circles.
